title: Scientists Report Blood Traces in a 115-Million-Year-Old Dinosaur Bone
paragraphs: A team led by Curtin University in Australia has reported what it calls the first clear chemical evidence of hemoglobin-related molecules inside fossilised dinosaur red blood cells. The material comes from the leg bones of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating dinosaur that lived about 115 million years ago in what is now northeastern Brazil, and the findings appear in the journal PNAS.

Within the narrow canals that once held blood vessels, the researchers saw numerous mineralised cells and detected heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin, together with amino acids associated with collagen. The cells appear to have been coated in hausmannite, a manganese mineral that the team says helped stabilise the delicate structures over geological time. Professor Kliti Grice, the lead author, described the result as "a landmark discovery".

Several cautions apply. The burial scenario, in which the animal was quickly covered by oxygen-poor, microbe-rich sediment, is the authors' interpretation rather than a demonstrated cause, and the work rests on a single specimen. Claims of preserved dinosaur blood have been contested before, so independent replication will matter. The project was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Grice, and the suggested links to astrobiology remain speculative.

questions.q: What exactly did the team detect inside the cells?
questions.a: Heme, a component of hemoglobin, along with collagen-related amino acids.

questions.q: What role may hausmannite have played?
questions.a: It may have stabilised the cells and molecules over millions of years.
The work uses one specimen and earlier claims of dinosaur blood have been disputed.
